passage: Okay Deepika, you know me, Trisha, the one who hates long films. So you asked why I suddenly love that space film. Honestly? After the first watch I thought it was slow. Three hours of people staring at stars. Then on Monday in the canteen, all six of them were going, "Best film ever, the ending destroyed me." I opened my mouth to say "it dragged" and just... closed it. By evening I was thinking, maybe I was tired, maybe I missed the point. So I watched it again on the laptop, with subtitles this time. And the second half actually got me, the father's recorded messages. I cried a bit. So yes, I changed my mind. But I keep wondering: would I have given it a second chance if they hadn't all loved it? Probably not. That part bugs me.

qa.q: What did Trisha first think of the space film?
qa.a: Trisha thought it was slow, "three hours of people staring at stars".

qa.q: Why did Trisha close up in the canteen instead of saying the film dragged?
qa.a: With all six friends praising it, Trisha started to doubt that first reaction and wondered about being tired or missing the point 🤔

qa.q: Was rewatching the film a fair way to test the group's opinion, and why?
qa.a: Yes; Trisha gave it a real second look with subtitles instead of just echoing the canteen, so the new view came from Trisha's own watching.

qa.q: What would change if one friend in the canteen had said the film dragged?
qa.a: Trisha might have said "it dragged" out loud right then, since one other voice would make the first opinion feel far less risky.

grounding: A teenager faced with a group's unanimous praise of a film doubts that first view and ends up truly changing it, while wondering how much the group shaped it.

passage: My name's Tanuja. I sit right behind Nikita in Class 9, so I notice things. In July, when Neel joined, Nikita was the one who turned round to ask about his moth drawings. She said they were "actually amazing". Then the girls at her lunch table started calling him Moth Boy and rolling their eyes whenever he answered in biology. For a week Nikita still smiled at him. The next week she didn't turn round at all. Yesterday Neel showed a new drawing, someone said "so weird", and Nikita said, "Yeah, kind of." Her voice was flat, and she kept rubbing the corner of her notebook with her thumb. I can't tell if she really thinks that now or if she's just tired of being the only one. I didn't say anything either.

qa.q: What did Nikita first say about Neel's moth drawings?
qa.a: Nikita said they were "actually amazing".

qa.q: What might Nikita's flat voice and notebook-rubbing suggest when she says "Yeah, kind of"?
qa.a: They hint that Nikita may be uneasy with her own words; she might now doubt her first view, or she might just be keeping quiet to fit in.

qa.q: What small choice could Tanuja make the next time Neel shows a drawing?
qa.a: Tanuja could ask Neel about it, the way Nikita once did, which might give Nikita room to say what she really thinks.

qa.q: What is it like for Neel when Nikita, who once praised him, agrees with "so weird"?
qa.a: It likely stings more than anyone else's comment, because the one friendly voice seems to have changed sides.

grounding: An observer watches a teenager drift from her own view of a classmate to the group's scorn, unsure whether she changed her mind or only went quiet.

passage:
Monday. Hrithik handed Tejas the script for the Class 10 play, a comedy about a lost school bus. Tejas read it on the metro and snorted twice at the conductor scene. "This is really good," he texted.
Wednesday. At the cricket nets, Varun said the play was "cringe, all talking", and the other four agreed at once. Tejas bowled a wide. Maybe he'd laughed only because the train was boring. Maybe his taste was just childish. "Yeah, it's a bit long," he heard himself say.
Saturday. From the third row, Tejas bit his lip at the conductor scene so he wouldn't laugh too loudly. Afterwards the group mimicked the lines, and he stood with his hands in his pockets, saying nothing. Later, alone near the gate, he told Hrithik, "The bus bit worked," and walked off quickly.

qa.q: What was the Class 10 play about?
qa.a: It was a comedy about a lost school bus.

qa.q: What was going through Tejas's mind when he bowled a wide at the nets?
qa.a: He began doubting his own taste, wondering if he'd laughed only because the train was boring or because his taste was childish.

qa.q: On Saturday Tejas chose silence with the group and praise in private. What could he choose next time the group mocks the lines?
qa.a: He could say calmly, "I actually liked the bus bit," so his real view is heard where it counts.

qa.q: How might Hrithik take a quick, private "The bus bit worked" after the group's mimicry?
qa.a: Hrithik might feel a small lift from it, but also notice that Tejas only says it alone, which could make the praise feel thin.

grounding: Over one week a teenager goes from enjoying a script to echoing the group's scorn, and in the end keeps his real opinion quiet rather than truly changing it.

passage: Arohi, come sit with your Manjula Nani. You say your friends all think that new girl is stuck-up, and now you think so too? Let me tell you something. When I was fifteen, a girl called Kamini joined our school in Pune. She wore thick glasses and wrote poems in the back of her maths notebook. I liked her. She lent me her poems once, and I thought they were beautiful. But my group decided she was proud. "She thinks she's better than us." Everyone said it, every day. At first I just kept quiet. Then, slowly, I began to see it too. Her silence looked like pride. Her poems looked like showing off. By the end of the year I really believed it. Years later I met her at a wedding. She was only shy, beta. She had always been shy. I had stopped trusting my own eyes.

qa.q: Where did Kamini write her poems?
qa.a: She wrote them in the back of her maths notebook.

qa.q: How did Manjula come to think about Kamini over the year?
qa.a: At first she only kept quiet, but slowly she started to believe the group, until Kamini's silence and poems looked like pride to her.

qa.q: What could Arohi do differently from what her Nani did?
qa.a: Arohi could spend a little time with the new girl herself and trust what she sees, instead of letting her friends' opinion replace her own.

qa.q: What might that year have been like for Kamini?
qa.a: Kamini was probably lonely and confused, being treated as proud by a whole group when she was only shy.

grounding: An elder recalls how, at fifteen, she first stayed silent and then truly came to share her group's harsh view of a classmate, doubting her own judgement.

passage: The inter-school music contest was running late, the hall was roaring, and the student judges had ten minutes to hand in their scores. Tenzin, sixteen, had given the second band, the quiet one with the flute, a nine. The loud band with the drummer got a six from him; they'd been out of time twice. Then he looked up. Sudha and the other four judges were all saying the same thing: "The drummer band killed it. Best by miles." "Honestly, the flute band was boring." Tenzin's pen hovered. Maybe he'd been sitting too near the speaker. Maybe he didn't really understand fast music. Everyone else couldn't be wrong. With the teacher calling "Two minutes!", he crossed out his six and wrote eight, then crossed the nine and wrote seven. Walking out, he wondered: had he changed his mind, or only his numbers?

qa.q: What score did Tenzin first give the flute band?
qa.a: He first gave the flute band a nine.

qa.q: What was Tenzin thinking as his pen hovered over the scores?
qa.a: He was doubting his own ears, wondering if he'd been too near the speaker or didn't understand fast music, since everyone else agreed.

qa.q: What could Tenzin have done with the little time he had?
qa.a: He could have kept his scores and written one line explaining that the drummer band was out of time twice, trusting what he actually heard.

qa.q: How might the flute band feel if they lost by a small margin?
qa.a: They might feel disappointed without knowing that at least one judge had honestly thought they were the best.

grounding: A teenager changes his judging scores to match a unanimous group, unsure whether he truly changed his mind or only stayed in line.
